effect_estimate.comment: Note internal contrast across model specifications reported by the authors: binary water-quality models (Table 2, p. 16) show Non-Designated Areas have higher odds of groundwater decline (OR = 1.20–1.54), whereas continuous contaminant models (Table 3, p. 17) report negative estimates for NDA on continuous decline rates (−1.770 to −10.46, p < 0.001). All figures are extracted directly from printed tables and text.
effect_estimate.value: Across 1,881 Arizona drinking water service areas, 20-year annual groundwater level changes ranged from −52.40 to −0.01 ft/year (−15.97 to −0.003 m/year) mainly outside Active Management Areas (AMAs), whereas gains (0.01 to 44.00 ft/year; 0.003 to 13.41 m/year) concentrated in regulated AMAs and urban centers. In binary water-quality logistic regressions of groundwater decline, unregulated Non-Designated Areas (NDAs) had higher odds of decline (20-yr nitrate model: est. = 0.300, p < 0.001, OR = 1.35; 10-yr: OR = 1.20; 20-yr arsenic model: est. = 0.431, p < 0.001, OR = 1.54; 10-yr: OR = 1.52), whereas Tribal SDWA primacy reduced decline odds (20-yr arsenic model: est. = −0.484, p < 0.001, OR = 0.62; 10-yr: OR = 0.69; 20-yr nitrate model: est. = −0.173, p < 0.001, OR = 0.84; 10-yr: OR = 0.89), with strong protective Tribal Primacy × Karst interactions (20-yr nitrate OR = 0.02, p = 0.007; arsenic OR = 0.00, p < 0.001). Unregulated Domestic Well Areas (DWAs vs. regulated CWS) showed slightly higher decline odds in binary nitrate models (20-yr est. = 0.033, p < 0.001, OR = 1.03; 10-yr OR = 1.01, p = 0.029). NDAs had higher odds of arsenic MCL exceedance (Estimate = 0.101, p = 0.004, OR = 1.11) and lower odds of nitrate MCL exceedance (Estimate = −0.733, p < 0.001, OR = 0.48). Higher Black population share increased 20-year decline odds (OR = 2.01 in nitrate model, OR = 1.88 in arsenic model, both p < 0.001), while renter-occupied housing was associated with lower decline odds (20-yr nitrate OR = 0.86, arsenic OR = 0.79, both p < 0.001).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at <= 2 by observational ecological cross-sectional design (JBI tool). Assigned 1 (documented association) because the study estimates statistical regressions linking spatial/regulatory boundary indicators (GMA designation, Tribal vs. State SDWA primacy, CWS vs. DWA supply type, and housing tenure shares) to groundwater decline and contaminant metrics without directly observing administrative procedures or enforcement processes in operation.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 8–10, Sections 2.3–2.4; PDF pp. 16–17, Tables 2–3; PDF pp. 25–26, Tables A1–A2

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines spatial service-area and groundwater management designations under the 1980 Groundwater Management Act (Active Management Areas vs. Non-Designated Areas; regulated CWS boundaries vs. unregulated exempt Domestic Well Areas), housing tenure composition (renter-occupied vs. fully owned homes), and fragmented regulatory enforcement/primacy across State vs. Tribal SDWA jurisdictions and regulated vs. unregulated groundwater zones.

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Observational spatial ecological study regressing period-summary groundwater level change rates (2001–2020 and 2011–2020) and contaminant indicators (1998–2019) on cross-sectional regulatory designations and 2020 Census sociodemographic shares across 1,881 service areas without a quasi-experimental intervention/comparator design (no DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, or panel FE). Matches JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies.

sample_size.value: 1,881 groundwater-supplied drinking water service areas (55.3% community water systems [CWS], 44.7% domestic well areas [DWAs]); 27,334 arsenic observations and 47,783 nitrate observations (1998–2019)

study_design.comment: Authors describe the design as a spatial ecological case study using areal apportionment, spatial autocorrelation/clustering, ANOVA, and multivariable mixed-effects and logistic regression models over 20-year (2001–2020) and 10-year (2011–2020) periods.
study_design.value: Observational spatial ecological study using geostatistical clustering (Moran's I, Getis-Ord Gi*, hierarchical and k-means clustering), ANOVA, and multivariable mixed-effects and logistic regression
